text: ation may be responsible.2 Other causative agents have included toxins such as dyes, insecticides, and turpentine.1 Initial supportive treatment of haemorrhagic cystitis in- volves increasing fluid intake to hydrate the bladder and dilute the concentration of any toxic agent in the urine. Symptomatic relief with antispasmodics and analgesics may be indicated.1 If haematuria does not improve or re- solve, intravesical treatment may be considered. This usu- ally begins with a continuous bladder irrigation of sodium chloride 0.9%, to remove existing clots.1-3 For bleeding that persists or worsens, other treatments have been de- scribed, mostly in case reports or small series.1-4 Alum irri- gation has been used for its astringent properties, but its effect is rarely permanent. Adverse effects include su- prapubic pain, fever, bladder spasm, and urinary retention or frequency; alum precipitation can block the catheter and aluminium toxicity may occur rarely. Silver nitrate instil- lation has a cauterising effect by coagulating proteins on the bladder mucosa, phenol causes a chemical cauterisa- tion, and formaldehyde hydrolyses protein on the bladder wall, coagulating tissue and controlling bleeding in the mucosa and submucosa. However, the duration of effect of these cauterising agents is often short, they are contra-indi- cated in patients with ureteric reflux, and treatments are painful, necessitating anaesthesia. Prostaglandins, such as alprostadil, carboprost, and dinoprostone, have been in- stilled into the bladder for a cytoprotective effect, to stim- ulate platelet aggregation, and to cause local vasoconstric- tion. There are also reports of successful systemic treatment in some cases that were refractory to intravesical therapy. Conjugated oestrogens have been given intravenously and orally.1 The antifibrinolytic drugs, aminocaproic acid1,2 and tranexamic acid2 have been given intravenously and orally; aminocaproic acid has also been given intravesical- ly. Oral pentosan polysulfate sodium has been used in ra- diation-induced haemorrhagic cystitis.3 Hyperbaric oxy- gen therapy increases tissue oxygenation and has been used particularly in radiation-induced haemorrhagic cysti- tis to treat radionecrosis and tissue ischaemia.3,4 Cryosur- gery using liquid nitrogen has been used rarely.1 In cases that do not respond to drug treatment, surgical op- tions include urinary diversion, internal iliac artery embol- isation, unilateral hypogastric artery ligation, and if all else fails, cystectomy.1-3 Hydrodistension, the application of pressure to the bladder wall by an inflated balloon, has also been used.4 However
